Thanks again for the RFP packet. A few clarifications from our security team so we can complete our vendor scoring:

1) BYOK escrow: can Redwood support a split-escrow model where Medicore holds one share, Redwood holds an encrypted backup share, and a certified third-party escrow agent holds the remainder? If so, what are the export/import controls and proof of destruction capabilities?

2) Ephemeral tenant keys: you mentioned optional ephemeral tenant keys for short-lived sessions. Please describe the lifecycle (generation, TTL, rotation cadence) and whether they are derived from a long-lived wrapping key or generated inside an HSM enclave.

3) KMIP proxy: does Redwood expose a KMIP front-end for our on-prem KMS to call, or do you offer a proxy that maps KMIP ops to your control plane? Any limitations on operations (e.g., no export, no clone)?

4) Emergency rotation & live failover: if we detect a compromise, how quickly can tenant wrapping keys be rotated across Dedicated pools and Private installations? Is there a documented playbook and a test harness you can run with our SREs?

5) TLS / mTLS: we need the supported cipher suites, OCSP stapling behavior, and whether Redwood supports client-certificate pinning for API connections originating from our VPC.

Can you provide short, actionable answers we can include in our security appendix?

Appreciate it — if easier, we can jump on a 30 min tech session.

Alex — thanks for the clear list. Answers below are concise; attached is a short appendix (redwood-ephemeral-key-workflow.pdf) and an attestation extract (attestation-claim-v1.txt). If you want a live run-through we can schedule a smoke test with our SREs.

Inline responses:

1) Split-escrow BYOK
- Supported: yes. We support a 3-party split-escrow pattern (tenant share + Redwood encrypted backup + third-party escrow).
- Export/Import controls: keys are wrapped with a customer-supplied wrapping key using AES-KW (RFC 3394) before any export. Exports require dual authorization (platform ops + customer API token) and are always logged and time-stamped.
- Proof of destruction: when a share is destroyed on our side we provide a signed destruction report (SHA-256 of the destroyed blob, operator IDs, and timestamp). Third-party escrow is coordinated per contract (we provide an encrypted payload and key handle only).

2) Ephemeral tenant keys
- Generation: ephemeral keys are generated inside HSM-backed partitions (FIPS 140-2 level 3 / 140-3 equivalent hardware) or inside a sealed software enclave for Private deployments that do not have HSMs.
- Lifecycle: default TTL is 5 minutes for session keys; configurable down to 1 minute or up to 24 hours with agreement.
- Rotation cadence: ephemeral keys rotate per-session; the tenant wrapping key (long-lived) rotates on a scheduled cadence (default 90 days) or immediately on-demand through our emergency rotation API.
- Derivation: ephemeral keys are either freshly generated inside the HSM or derived via HKDF from a tenant wrapping key with per-session salt depending on customer policy. We never export raw ephemeral private material.

3) KMIP proxy
- Options: we provide a KMIP adapter that can act as a proxy for on-prem KMS calls (read-only and key-use ops) and map KMIP Create/Locate/Get to our control plane.
- Limitations: KMIP export operations are blocked by default (no key material export). Administration operations require RBAC and a scoped service account. Audit events map KMIP operations to internal event IDs for traceability.

4) Emergency rotation & failover
- Rotation SLA: in Hosted/Dedicated, tenant wrapping keys can be rotated within a 2 hour RTO for metadata-only rotation (rekey handle swap) and within 6 hours for full re-wrap of active caches with force reissue. For Private deployments runbook-driven rotation times depend on customer environment; we have a tested playbook that typically completes within 8–24 hours.
- Playbook & test harness: attached appendix includes a condensed playbook. We offer a 2-hour tabletop and a 4-hour hands-on drill with your SREs for an additional services engagement.

5) TLS / mTLS
- Cipher suites: TLS 1.2 (restricted set) and TLS 1.3 supported. Preferred TLS 1.3 suites (TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256, TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384).
- OCSP: OCSP stapling is supported on our public endpoints; we also provide short-lived leaf certs for Dedicated/Private (if requested) to reduce OCSP latency.
- Client cert pinning: supported for VPC-originating API endpoints. We support mutual TLS with cert rotation via our API and client cert pinning at the route level.

If this level of detail is fine, Jordan can add a short KMIP appendix and a playbook checklist (I included those in cc).

> > "3) KMIP proxy - Options: we provide a KMIP adapter that can act as a proxy for on-prem KMS calls (read-only and key-use ops) and map KMIP Create/Locate/Get to our control plane."
>
> KMIP appendix (high level):
> - We implement KMIP 1.4 subset; the proxy accepts Create, Get, Locate, Register, and Use operations.
> - Export and Key Material Extract are explicitly disabled (we return KMIP Error: OperationNotSupported).
> - For on-prem integrations we recommend a short-lived service account with scoped credentials and mutual TLS between the proxy and customer KMS.
> - Performance: proxy introduces ~5–12ms median latency on control plane ops in our tests; policy evaluation and audit logging are async to reduce path latency.
>
> Additional notes on emergency key handling:
> - Cache evictions: we have a global cache invalidation API for Dedicated that triggers background re-wraps and forces new session tokens; it's controlled via a dual-auth flow.
> - Key derivation: when deriving ephemeral session keys via HKDF we use SHA-256 with a 32-byte salt and include a context string (customer-id, session-id, timestamp) to prevent cross-tenant reuse.
>
